title: Daylighting-Bias and Biophilia: Quantifying the Impacts of Daylighting and Views on Occupants Health

findings.mechanism: innate affiliation with nature, restorative qualities
findings.source: VIEW QUALITY PREFERENCE ANALYSIS text, Figure 9
findings.quote: Results indicate an agreement of those surveyed to rank natural views at the top of their preference with wild forest like settings to be more preferred than manicured and structured landscaping.

findings.consequent: Employee preference over no outdoor view
findings.mechanism: diminish stress and combat the feeling of confinement inside offices
findings.quote: Employees with no views in internal facing offices were reportedly interested in any view over their windowless offices.

findings.antecedent: No outdoor view from office (39% of employees)
findings.consequent: Use of natural images (posters, postcards, computer screensavers)
findings.mechanism: seeking connection to nature as a coping mechanism
findings.quote: Employees with no views and windows in their offices (39% of employees) had posters, postcards, and computer screensavers with images of natural scenes.

findings.antecedent: No outdoor views (Group 5) or low-rated urban views (Group 4)
findings.mechanism: lack of restorative views leading to poorer health outcomes
findings.source: Figure 10, LIGHTING AND VIEWS QUALITY IMPACTS text
findings.quote: The above figures all confirm a strong trend of increased sick leave days due to physical sickness of employees in group 5 (no views) and group 4(urban low rated views).

findings.antecedent: No outdoor views (Group 5) or low-rated urban views (Group 4)
findings.source: Figure 11, LIGHTING AND VIEWS QUALITY IMPACTS text
findings.quote: In addition, offices with no views or low ranking views of urban structures were highly correlated with the perception of low lighting quality, reported physical discomfort...

findings.antecedent: Lowest ranking views or no views (Groups 3, 4 & 5)
findings.consequent: Seeking better views by walking around offices or visiting other office settings during breaks
findings.source: Figure 13, LIGHTING AND VIEWS QUALITY IMPACTS text
findings.quote: employees with lowest ranking views or no views (groups 3, 4 & 5), have been consistently seeking better views by walking around their offices and visiting other office settings with better view ratings (group 5).

findings.antecedent: No outdoor views (Group 5) or low-rated urban views (Group 4)
findings.mechanism: perception of poor lighting quality in absence of views
findings.source: Figure 14, LIGHTING AND VIEWS QUALITY IMPACTS text
findings.quote: In addition, offices with no views or low ranking views of urban structures were highly correlated with the perception of low lighting quality...

findings.mechanism: lack of restorative views, increased stress
measures of lighting quality and view were related
findings.quote: As would be expected, the measures of lighting quality and view were related (r = 0.43, p < 0.001).

findings.antecedent: Poor Lighting Quality (PLQ) rating and Poor View Rating (PVR) rating
findings.mechanism: combined impact of environmental factors on health
findings.quote: Taken together, the two variables explained 6.5% of the variation in sick leave use, which was statistically significant.

findings.mechanism: architectural and design elements influencing daylight and views
findings.quote: The effect of glazing area is as predicted; with fewer sick days used when glazing area is larger (negative coefficient).

findings.antecedent: Glazing area (sq. ft.), Poor Lighting Quality (PLQ) rating, and Poor View Rating (PVR) rating
findings.mechanism: combined impact of architectural and design elements on health
findings.quote: The R square value with the 3 variables in the prediction equation is 0.09. This says that almost 10% of the variation in the use of sick leave days is explained by these architectural and design elements; namely glazing area, lighting quality, and views quality.
